AI Contract Drafting System

A controlled NDA drafting engine that combines deterministic clause assembly with an AI-powered intake layer. The system generates legally structured contracts from plain-English descriptions — no hallucinated legal language, no freeform text generation. Every clause traces back to a governed source.

The Problem
1

Legal drafting is slow

NDAs are among the most common legal documents, yet they're still manually assembled. Attorneys spend ~64% of their time on document busywork — over 100 hours per month.

2

LLMs hallucinate legal text

Free-generation with language models is risky for legal documents. Hallucinated clauses can have real legal consequences — a governed drafting approach is the safer path.

3

No reusable clause data

Legal teams have no structured, auditable clause library. Every draft starts from scratch or from a loosely maintained Word template.

Architecture

The system is designed in four layers — data, config, engine, and AI — so each layer can evolve independently. The deterministic backbone was built first; the AI layer was added on top without breaking the assembler.

How It Works
1

User describes the contract

Plain English: "We need a unilateral NDA between Acme Corp and Beta Ventures for 3 years under Connecticut law."

2

AI extracts canonical fields

Ollama (Qwen 3 4B, running locally) maps the request into the fixed 12-field schema. Returns evidence for each extracted value.

3

Follow-up for missing fields

The system asks only for what it couldn't confidently extract — entity details, email addresses, dispute resolution method.

4

Deterministic assembly

Clauses selected from the governed library, placeholders filled algorithmically, contract assembled in fixed order. No LLM-generated legal text.

5

Validated NDA output

Complete contract draft with zero unresolved placeholders, plus a key terms summary and validation report.

Key Design Decisions
Adopted

Fixed canonical schema

The AI fills a fixed questionnaire schema — it does not generate or modify the schema at runtime. We tested agent-generated schemas and they caused field-name drift, missing required fields, and broken assembly.

Adopted

Evidence-based extraction

Every extracted value must have supporting evidence copied from the user's own words. If there's no evidence, the system asks a follow-up instead of guessing.

Rejected

Agent-owned questionnaire

Letting the LLM generate the questionnaire structure caused schema drift, merged fields, and omitted fields the assembler needed. The agent fills the schema — it doesn't own it.

Adopted

Deterministic-first architecture

We built the drafting engine before adding AI. Every deterministic step is a clear handoff point for future AI orchestration — the agent builds on top, not the other way around.

AI Intake Testing

We ran 6 test scenarios ranging from fully specified prompts to conversational/indirect language. The deterministic assembler passed every time — the variable was AI extraction quality.

Pass
Test 1 — Fully specified unilateral

All fields provided. AI extracted everything correctly, zero follow-ups needed.

Partial
Test 2 — Partially specified unilateral

Missing entity details and emails. Follow-up behavior was inconsistent — sometimes asked correctly, sometimes tried to fill values.

Pass
Test 3 — Role-based (implied unilateral)

"Acme wants to disclose to Beta..." — AI correctly inferred unilateral type from context.

Pass
Test 4 — Fully specified mutual

Mutual NDA path working end-to-end with all fields extracted.

Pass
Test 5 — Partially specified mutual

Missing fields correctly identified. Follow-up questions asked and answers accepted.

Fail
Test 6 — Conversational / indirect

Extractor returned almost nothing from natural language. System fell back to asking nearly every question manually.

Conclusion: The deterministic assembler is not the bottleneck. The remaining challenge is AI extraction robustness on indirect and conversational prompts.
